opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the core problem is that when you look inside a language model, you're staring at these enormous vectors, thousands of dimensions in the residual stream at every layer and every token position, and individual neurons mostly don't mean anything clean on their own. They're polysemantic: one neuron might fire for a bunch of unrelated concepts. So if you just look at raw activations, it's really hard to tell a story about what the model is doing.

The approach we've taken has two main steps. The first is to change the basis we're looking in. We train a replacement model, in our case something called a cross-layer transcoder, that learns to reconstruct what the model's MLP layers are computing, but using a much larger set of sparse features. The idea is that each of those features is more interpretable. You get features that correspond to things like "this is a capital city," "the text is in French," or "we're about to need a word that rhymes with 'rabbit.'" And because they're sparse, only a small number are active on any given prompt.

The second step is the attribution graph itself. For a specific prompt, we trace how those active features influence each other, starting from the input tokens, flowing through intermediate features, and ending at the model's output logits. We freeze certain things, like the attention patterns, so the interactions between features become linear and we can compute direct effects exactly. What you end up with is a graph: nodes are features, edges are how much one feature contributed to another. That gives you something like a wiring diagram for that one computation.

Even then, the raw graph is way too big to read, so we prune it down to the most important paths, and then a human, or increasingly some automated tooling, looks at the features, groups related ones into what we call supernodes, and tries to tell the story. A classic example is the two-hop question: "the capital of the state containing Dallas is..." You can see the model activate a "Texas" representation internally and then use that to get to "Austin." It's genuinely doing a multi-step reasoning step in its activations, not just memorizing the answer.

The important caveat is that this is a hypothesis-generating tool. The replacement model isn't perfect; there's always some error we can't explain. So we always validate by going back to the real model and intervening: suppress the "Texas" feature, or swap it for "California," and check whether the output changes the way the graph predicts. When the interventions line up, you get real confidence that you've found part of the actual mechanism. When they don't, that's informative too, because it tells you where the method is missing something.

r001.rationale: The response describes edges as feature contributions and says direct effects can be computed, but it does not identify them as dot products between high-dimensional computation vectors.

r002.rationale: The response says sparse features are more interpretable, but it does not state that interpreting the graph does not require understanding the underlying high-dimensional vectors.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the core problem is that if you just look at the raw activations in a model, you're staring at millions of numbers per token, and the individual neurons don't really mean anything on their own. They're polysemantic, they fire for a dozen unrelated things at once. So the first move is to replace that basis with something more interpretable.

The way we do that is with what we call a replacement model. We train these sparse dictionaries, cross-layer transcoders, that take the model's residual stream and decompose it into features. Each feature is meant to correspond to a single concept the model is using, like "this is a capital city," or "we're inside a rhyming couplet," or "the user is asking for a refusal." Instead of thirty thousand neurons at a layer, you might have a few dozen features that are actually active on a given token, and you can read each of them.

Once you have that, the attribution graph is really just asking: for a particular output the model produced, which features mattered, and how did they influence each other? So you take a prompt, you run it forward, and you compute how much each active feature contributed to the features downstream of it, all the way out to the logit for the token the model picked. You get a directed graph. Nodes are features at particular token positions, edges are how strongly one caused the next.

And then the honest part of the method is pruning. The full graph is still enormous, so you keep only the paths that account for most of the effect on the output, and you throw the rest away. What's left is usually something a person can actually look at: maybe a few hundred nodes, often organized into a handful of pathways. You can trace it and say, okay, the model saw "Dallas," that activated a Texas feature, Texas plus "capital" activated an Austin feature, and that drove the output.

The thing I'd stress is that the graph is a hypothesis, not a proof. It's generated from an approximation of the model, and the approximation has error. So we always follow up with interventions. If the graph says this feature is doing the work, you go into the real model, suppress that feature, and check that the output changes the way you predicted. When it does, you've got something. When it doesn't, you've learned the replacement model is misleading you somewhere, and that's useful too.

It's a bit like doing a dissection where you're only allowed to look at a cast of the organism instead of the organism itself. The cast is good enough to see the major structures, but you have to go back and poke the real thing before you believe what you're seeing.

r001.rationale: The response describes edges as showing how strongly one feature caused another, but does not say they represent dot products between high-dimensional computation vectors.

r002.rationale: The response explains replacing raw activations with interpretable features, but does not state that understanding the underlying high-dimensional vectors is unnecessary for interpreting the graph.

astra-6.text:
The idea is to move from looking at individual neurons to looking at features that have a more understandable meaning. A model’s internal state is a very high-dimensional vector, and the information you care about can be spread across many dimensions. So we try to identify features that correspond to recognizable concepts or patterns, and then trace how those features influence one another during a particular computation.

An attribution graph gives you a view of that process. The nodes represent features, and the edges represent estimated influences between them. You can start from an output and work backward: What contributed to this answer? What contributed to those intermediate features? That can turn an otherwise opaque computation into something you can formulate a hypothesis about.

The important caveat is that a readable graph isn’t automatically a faithful explanation. It’s an approximation, and it can leave things out. So you want to test the story it suggests by intervening—suppressing or changing a feature, for example—and checking whether the model’s behavior changes in the way you predicted. That combination of tracing and testing is what makes this useful.

r001.rationale: The response says edges represent estimated influences, but does not explain that they represent dot products between high-dimensional computation vectors.

r002.rationale: The response describes using features to make computation more understandable, but does not state that interpreting the graph does not require understanding the underlying high-dimensional vectors.

sol-6.1.text:
One way to think about an attribution graph is as a simplified map of the computation the model is doing. Inside a language model, you have these very high-dimensional vectors, and it’s hard to look at those directly and understand what they mean. So we try to identify interpretable features—patterns that correspond to concepts or behaviors—and then trace how those features influence one another as the model produces an answer.

For example, if you ask a model for the capital of Texas, you might see features related to Texas feeding into features related to Austin, which then contribute to the output. The graph gives you a way to formulate a hypothesis about how the model arrived at that answer.

The important caveat is that this is an approximation. We’re not capturing every part of the computation, and a connection in the graph isn’t, by itself, a complete causal explanation. So we also intervene: suppress a feature or change its activation and see whether the model’s behavior changes in the way the graph predicts. That’s how we start moving from a visualization that looks plausible to an explanation we can actually test.

r001.rationale: The response describes graph connections as features influencing one another, but does not explain that edges represent dot products between high-dimensional computation vectors.

r002.rationale: It says the vectors are hard to interpret directly and describes identifying interpretable features, but does not state that understanding the vectors is unnecessary for interpreting the graph.
